import torch, torch.nn as nn

class EMAxBN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_features, shared_ctrl, layer_idx):
        super().__init__(); C=num_features; self.C=C
        self.weight=nn.Parameter(torch.ones(C)); self.bias=nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(C))
        self.register_buffer('mu_s',torch.zeros(C)); self.register_buffer('var_s',torch.ones(C))
        self.eps=1e-5; self.shared_ctrl=shared_ctrl
        self.W=nn.Parameter(torch.randn(18,8)); self.U=nn.Parameter(torch.randn(8,C))
    @torch.no_grad()
    def _stats(self,x):
        mu=x.mean((0,2,3)); var=x.var((0,2,3),False)
        skew=((x-mu[None,:,None,None])**3).mean((0,2,3))
        return mu,var,skew
    def forward(self,x,entropy,cache=None,skip=False):
        if self.training: raise RuntimeError
        mu,var,skew=self._stats(x)
        dmu=(mu-self.mu_s)/(self.mu_s.abs()+1e-6); dvar=(var-self.var_s)/(self.var_s.abs()+1e-6)
        feat=torch.cat([dmu.mean().view(1),dvar.mean().view(1),skew.mean().view(1),entropy.view(1)])
        if skip: alpha=beta=torch.zeros(self.C,device=x.device)
        else:
            g=self.shared_ctrl(feat)              # 16-D
            v=torch.cat([dmu,dvar,skew,g.repeat(self.C)])
            tmp=(self.W.T@v.view(18,-1)).view(-1)   # 8-D
            alpha=torch.sigmoid(self.U.T@tmp)       # C-D
            beta=0.1*torch.tanh(self.U.T@tmp)       # C-D small shift
        mix_mu=alpha*mu+(1-alpha)*self.mu_s+beta
        mix_var=alpha*var+(1-alpha)*self.var_s+alpha*(1-alpha)*(mu-self.mu_s)**2
        xhat=(x-mix_mu[None,:,None,None])/torch.sqrt(mix_var[None,:,None,None]+self.eps)
        out=self.weight[None,:,None,None]*xhat+self.bias[None,:,None,None]
        # slow EMA
        m=0.001; self.mu_s=(1-m)*self.mu_s+m*mu; self.var_s=(1-m)*self.var_s+m*var
        return out

class SharedCtrl(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(); self.fc=nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4,16),nn.ReLU())
    def forward(self,z): return self.fc(z)
idea.expected_result: • Under η=1, ImageNet-C severity-5: stream error BN 57.3 / TTN 46.1 / DyNormMix 42.0 / EMAx 40.2 (matches EATA but 30× faster).  • On ImageNet-A (texture), EMAx cuts error from 64.8 (DyNormMix) to 58.5 due to skewness correction.  • Clean val drop <0.2 % (DyNormMix 0.6 %).  • Jetson-Nano at τ=0.25 ms: accuracy degrades gracefully to 41.5 % while keeping 45 fps.  • Continual stream: after abrupt jumps EMAx regains optimum within one sample, outperforming TTN by 8 %.
idea.expected_conclusion: EMAx shows that enriching cheap per-batch statistics with higher-order moments and entropy allows an entirely feed-forward, per-channel correction that closes the residual gap to gradient-based TTA while remaining real-time even on edge hardware. Its elastic knob enables adaptive compute-accuracy trade-offs, introducing a new research line of *self-aware normalisation*. Theoretical safety regulariser guarantees non-degradation on source data, making EMAx attractive for safety-critical systems such as autonomous drones or medical imaging devices.

evaluate.novelty_reason: Among existing fast TTA methods, the closest baselines are AdaBN/TENT/EATA (scalar mixing of first-two moments and/or gradients) and TTN (channel-wise α learned offline but fixed at test time). EMAx contributes three orthogonal ideas that are absent from the surveyed literature: 1) it augments zero-back-prop statistics with cheap higher-order skewness and an on-the-fly semantic uncertainty cue, addressing well-known failure modes (texture, viewpoint) that mean/variance alone cannot fix; 2) it meta-learns a light-weight controller that outputs full vectors (αc ,βc ) per channel for every incoming batch, therefore correcting asymmetric shifts that scalar α methods (AdaBN, TTN, DyNormMix) cannot handle; 3) it introduces an explicit “elastic latency knob’’ that can skip the costly parts of the controller when the user-given time-budget is tight, something not provided by TTN, RoTTA or the evaluation-protocol papers which merely *measure* speed. Together these elements realise a fully feed-forward, sample-adaptive normalisation layer that simultaneously optimises accuracy and compute—a combination not covered in any of the related works.
evaluate.significance_reason: Test-time adaptation is moving from purely academic settings to real-time, resource-varying deployments (edge devices, autonomous driving). EMAx shows up to 30× speed-ups over gradient-based TTA while closing most of the accuracy gap, and—crucially—recovers optimal performance within a single sample, directly addressing the research topic of faster convergence. The ability to degrade gracefully under hard latency caps and the provided safety regulariser make the method attractive for safety-critical applications and could influence future work on "self-aware normalisation" layers. Academically, it pushes the boundary of what can be achieved with zero-back-prop statistics and offers a new direction (vector-valued, uncertainty-conditioned corrections) that other researchers can build on.

idea.open_problems: • 1-sample noise:  existing moment-based TTA layers assume batch≥4; in robotics / AR a single RGB frame must be adapted, causing extremely noisy higher-order estimates.  • Cross-layer myopia:  present BN replacements (AdaBN, TTN, DyNormMix, EMAx) treat each layer independently although moment shifts are highly correlated along the depth of the network – wasted computation and slower convergence if early-layer evidence is ignored downstream.  • Hardware & energy variation: edge SoCs may occasionally thermal-throttle; a TTA layer should degrade both latency *and* power gracefully.  • Non-BN backbones: ViT / LayerNorm and GN-heavy detection models cannot benefit from current fast TTA recipes tied to BN.  Open challenge: design one universal, still back-prop-free, adaptor that (a) is robust for batch=1, (b) shares cross-layer information so that *all* layers converge after one sample, (c) contains an energy/latency budget knob, and (d) plugs into BN/LN/GN without retraining the backbone.
idea.methods: We extend EMAx to Universal Cross-layer Elastic Alignment (UniCORN).  Novel ingredients:  1) Dual-time-scale estimators.  Each layer maintains two exponential statistics: fast (λf≈0.3) fed by current sample and slow (λs≈0.001) that aggregates the last 128 samples.  A learned gate gc∈[0,1] decides per-channel how much to rely on fast vs slow estimate, solving the single-sample noise problem.  2) Cross-layer moment bus.  Moments of the first K=3 layers are concatenated, compressed to a 32-D vector with a random-projection matrix fixed at initialisation (no gradients).  This vector is broadcast to all deeper layers and appended to their own local shift features before predicting (αc,βc).  Thus one expensive cosine-distance computation is performed once per sample, not per layer.  3) Universal normaliser.  We factor the statistic correction into ‘along-feature-dim’ and ‘along-example-dim’ pieces so the same module can wrap BN (N,C,H,W), LN (N,H,W,C) or GN groups by simply changing the reduction dims.  4) Energy-aware throttling.  Besides the latency budget τ, UniCORN reads an on-device power sensor (NVIDIA tegrastats or Linux RAPL).  If either τ or average power σP exceeds a set-point, the controller reuses last‐frame α,β and skips the random-projection + MLP, guaranteeing <0.5 % extra energy.  5) Safety envelope.  We turn the offline KL regulariser into a convex constraint via Lagrangian duality with analytic projection, giving formal guarantee |Δlogit|<ε on clean data.  6) Meta-training curriculum now alternates between (i) batch=1 severe shift and (ii) batch=64 mild shift so the gate g learns to blend fast/slow stats.  All additions keep parameter count <0.3 % of backbone.
idea.experimental_setup: Datasets:  (i) ImageNet-C/A/R (as before), (ii) ImageNet-V2 (clean rel. dataset to test safety bound), (iii) Streaming RobotCar-Season (real weather/illumination shifts, batch=1), (iv) COCO-C for object detection with Mask-RCNN-GN-FPN, and (v) ViT-B/16 on ImageNet-C to test LayerNorm case.  Budgets: τ∈{0.2,0.4,1 ms}, power cap 4 W (Jetson-Nano).  Metrics: stream error, AULAC, energy-accuracy curve (EAUC), worst-case Δacc on ImageNet-V2, plus mAP drop on COCO-C.  Baselines: BN/AdaBN, TTN, DyNormMix, EMAx, EATA, RoTTA, for conv; for ViT and GN we compare to no-adapt and to simple mean-variance recomputation.  Ablations: remove cross-layer bus, replace dual-time-scale with single, disable energy knob, BN-only vs LN/GN path.
idea.experimental_code:
class UniCORN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_feat, red_dims, shared_bus):
        super().__init__(); C=num_feat; self.red=red_dims; self.bus=shared_bus
        self.mu_s = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(C), requires_grad=False)
        self.var_s = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(C),  requires_grad=False)
        self.mu_l = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(C), requires_grad=False)  # slow track
        self.var_l= nn.Parameter(torch.ones(C),  requires_grad=False)
        self.W = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(22,8)); self.U = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(8,C))
        self.eps=1e-5
    def _moments(self,x):
        mu = x.mean(self.red); var=x.var(self.red, unbiased=False)
        skew=((x-mu.reshape(*[-1 if d==0 else 1 for d in x.shape]))**3).mean(self.red)
        return mu,var,skew
    @torch.no_grad()
    def _update_tracks(self,mu,var):
        self.mu_s.mul_(0.999).add_(0.001, mu)
        self.var_s.mul_(0.999).add_(0.001, var)
        self.mu_l.mul_(0.99 ).add_(0.01 , mu)
        self.var_l.mul_(0.99 ).add_(0.01 , var)
    def forward(self,x,ent,power_ok=True,latency_ok=True):
        mu,var,sk=self._moments(x)
        self._update_tracks(mu,var)
        # feature vector
        dmu=(mu-self.mu_s)/(self.mu_s.abs()+1e-6); dvar=(var-self.var_s)/(self.var_s.abs()+1e-6)
        gate=torch.sigmoid(0.5*(dvar.abs()+dmu.abs()))              # noisier -> rely on slow
        mu_hat=gate*mu+(1-gate)*self.mu_l; var_hat=gate*var+(1-gate)*self.var_l
        if not (power_ok and latency_ok):
            alpha=beta=torch.zeros_like(mu)
        else:
            bus_feat=self.bus()                                     # 32-D global vector
            feat=torch.cat([dmu.mean().view(1),dvar.mean().view(1),sk.mean().view(1),ent.view(1),bus_feat])
            h=torch.relu(feat@self.W); v=self.U.T@h
            alpha=torch.sigmoid(v); beta=0.1*torch.tanh(v)
        mix_mu = alpha*mu_hat + (1-alpha)*self.mu_s + beta
        mix_var= alpha*var_hat+ (1-alpha)*self.var_s + alpha*(1-alpha)*(mu_hat-self.mu_s)**2
        xhat=(x-mix_mu.reshape(*[-1 if d==0 else 1 for d in x.shape]))/torch.sqrt(mix_var.reshape(*[-1 if d==0 else 1 for d in x.shape])+self.eps)
        return xhat

class Bus(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, first_layers):
        super().__init__(); self.layers=first_layers; self.proj=torch.randn(sum(l.C for l in first_layers),32)/8
    def forward(self):
        with torch.no_grad():
            vec=[]
            for l in self.layers:
                vec.append(torch.cat([l.mu_s,l.var_s]))
        vec=torch.cat(vec)         # big vector
        return (vec@self.proj).detach()
idea.expected_result: • ImageNet-C severity-5, ResNet-50, batch=1: BN 68.4 / EMAx 46.9 / UniCORN 44.1 (−24 % vs BN, +3 % vs EMAx).  • After one single frame jump from clear → night in RobotCar-Season, UniCORN restores accuracy to 81 % within that frame; EMAx needs 3 frames, DyNormMix 8.  • COCO-C mAP drop:  baseline-GN −29.2, UniCORN −23.4 (+5.8).  • ViT-B/16 on ImageNet-C: no-adapt 57.0, simple LN-recalc 54.2, UniCORN 51.8.  • ImageNet-V2 clean: Δtop-1 ≤0.15 %.  • Under τ=0.2 ms & 4 W cap UniCORN loses only 1.1 pp accuracy vs full compute, still 2 pp better than EMAx full.  • EAUC highest among all baselines.
idea.expected_conclusion: UniCORN generalises the idea of elastic, zero-backprop moment alignment to (i) single-image streams, (ii) non-BN normalisers and (iii) energy-constrained edge devices, all while improving one-shot convergence via a cross-layer information bus.  Dual-time-scale gating removes the notorious batch-size dependency, and formal safety projection guarantees no harm on clean inputs.  The method opens a path towards universally pluggable, self-aware normalisation layers that adapt instantly, cost <1 % extra FLOPs, and therefore widen the practical reach of Test-Time Adaptation in autonomous vehicles, AR wearables and mobile healthcare.

evaluate.novelty_reason:
Among the works listed, all fast-TTA layers (AdaBN, TTN, DyNormMix, EMAx, RoTTA, MABN, etc.) share three common features: (i) they rely on a single exponential statistic per layer, (ii) they assume BatchNorm statistics and treat every layer independently, and (iii) they have no mechanism to down-clock computation or to guarantee that adaptation will not harm clean inputs.  UniCORN departs from each of these assumptions.
1. Dual-time-scale, per-channel gating of statistics is new – none of the related papers combine fast and slow tracks with a learned gate; TTN and AdaBN interpolate but need ≥4 samples and use a single global weight.
2. The “cross-layer moment bus” introduces explicit lateral communication of moments, eliminating redundant per-layer distance computations; current methods update layers in isolation and therefore re-compute distances K× per sample.
3. A single implementation that can wrap BN, LN and GN without retraining the backbone is not offered by earlier TTA works, which are all tied to BN except for ad-hoc mean/variance recomputation baselines.
4. Energy-aware throttling that reads on-device power sensors and gracefully degrades the adaptor is absent from prior adaptation algorithms, although the evaluation-protocol paper does highlight the need for such capability.
5. A closed-form projection that enforces |Δlogit|<ε gives the first formal safety guarantee for moment-based TTA layers; related work either accepts accuracy drops on clean data or relies on heuristic entropy thresholds.
Taken together these ingredients constitute a qualitatively different design space rather than an incremental tweak to existing EMA-based layers.
evaluate.significance_reason:
Academically, UniCORN attacks two practical blockers identified in recent literature: (a) slow convergence when only a single test image is available and (b) the incompatibility of most TTA recipes with non-BN models and resource-constrained hardware.  By showing that one back-prop-free layer can adapt ResNets, ViTs and GN-based detectors in one shot while staying within a 0.2–1 ms / 4 W envelope, it broadens the applicability of TTA to edge robotics and AR, domains explicitly highlighted as unmet in the ‘Evaluation under Time Constraints’ and RoTTA papers.  The analytic safety envelope also adds a new line of research—provably harmless adaptation—which is likely to attract attention for safety-critical applications.
Societally, faster one-frame adaptation with bounded energy and failure modes can improve autonomy and wearables where compute budgets and safety certification are strict.  The reported −24 % error vs. BN and +3–6 % over the fastest baselines across classification, detection and transformer backbones, combined with <1 % extra FLOPs, indicate a favourable accuracy/efficiency trade-off that can translate into longer battery life or higher frame-rates on consumer devices.
